title: Can the `main()` method be overridden (static method hiding vs overriding)?
shortTitle: Can the main method be overridden?

s1_definition.profdef: No, the main method cannot be overridden, because overriding applies only to instance methods and is resolved dynamically at runtime based on the actual object's type, whereas main is static and static methods are never overridden. When a subclass declares a static method with the same signature as a static method in its superclass, that is method hiding, not overriding: the two methods are independent, and which one runs is decided at compile time by the declared type of the reference, not by any runtime object. Because the JVM entry point is specifically the static main of the class named on the command line, there is no polymorphic dispatch involved at all; the launcher simply calls the static main of that exact class.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, overriding is like a specialist branch replacing head office's standard procedure with its own version, where which procedure actually runs depends on which real branch you walked into, decided on the spot. Static methods do not work that way. A static method named main in a subclass branch does not replace the parent branch's main; instead each branch keeps its own separate notice posted on its own wall, and which notice you read depends only on which branch's name you looked up on the directory, decided in advance, not on any live person in front of you. So the child branch's main simply hides, meaning sits beside, the parent's main, and the JVM reads whichever branch's main matches the exact class name you asked it to start.
s1_definition.oneliner: main cannot be overridden because it is static; a same-signature static method in a subclass hides the parent's rather than overriding it, and hiding is resolved at compile time by reference type while overriding is resolved at runtime by object type.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** No, the main method cannot be overridden, because overriding applies only to instance methods and is resolved dynamically at runtime based on the actual object's type, whereas main is static and static methods are never overridden. When a subclass declares a static method with the same signature as a static method in its superclass, that is method hiding, not overriding: the two methods are independent, and which one runs is decided at compile time by the declared type of the reference, not by any runtime object. Because the JVM entry point is specifically the static main of the class named on the command line, there is no polymorphic dispatch involved at all; the launcher simply calls the static main of that exact class.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, overriding is like a specialist branch replacing head office's standard procedure with its own version, where which procedure actually runs depends on which real branch you walked into, decided on the spot. Static methods do not work that way. A static method named main in a subclass branch does not replace the parent branch's main; instead each branch keeps its own separate notice posted on its own wall, and which notice you read depends only on which branch's name you looked up on the directory, decided in advance, not on any live person in front of you. So the child branch's main simply hides, meaning sits beside, the parent's main, and the JVM reads whichever branch's main matches the exact class name you asked it to start.

**One line to remember:** main cannot be overridden because it is static; a same-signature static method in a subclass hides the parent's rather than overriding it, and hiding is resolved at compile time by reference type while overriding is resolved at runtime by object type.

sections.s2_technical:
Overriding is a runtime mechanism that applies only to instance methods. When a subclass provides an instance method with the same signature as its superclass, a call through a superclass reference is dispatched at runtime to the subclass version based on the actual object. This dynamic dispatch is the heart of polymorphism. The main method, being static, is bound to the class, not to any instance, so it is excluded from this mechanism entirely.

When a subclass declares a static method with the same name and parameters as a static method in the superclass, the Java Language Specification calls this hiding, not overriding. The two static methods coexist as separate members. Which one executes is determined at compile time by the type of the reference used to call it, not by the runtime type of any object. So if a parent class Parent has a static greet and a child class Child hides it with its own static greet, then calling through a reference typed as Parent runs Parent's version even if the object is actually a Child, which is the opposite of overriding behavior.

Applied to main, this means a subclass can declare its own public static void main of a String array, and it simply hides the parent's main; it does not override it. There is no polymorphism because the JVM launcher does not dispatch dynamically; it invokes the static main of precisely the class you named on the command line. If you run the parent class, the parent's main runs; if you run the child class, the child's main runs. Each is selected by the class name, which is a compile-time-style, static selection, never a runtime object-based one.

Several senior points matter. First, the telltale sign of hiding versus overriding is the at-Override annotation: placing it on a static method that merely hides a parent's static method is a compile error, because at-Override asserts genuine overriding, which static methods cannot do. Second, hiding does not respect dynamic type, so it is a common source of confusion and is generally discouraged for ordinary static methods because it looks like overriding but behaves differently. Third, an instance method cannot have the same signature as an inherited static method and vice versa; you cannot turn a static method into an instance method in a subclass, which would be a compile error, so main stays static throughout a hierarchy. Fourth, in practice banking applications rarely build class hierarchies around main; instead each runnable entry class has its own main, and the lack of overriding is exactly what guarantees that running a specific launcher class runs that class's own startup logic predictably. Understanding hiding versus overriding prevents the classic trap of expecting a subclass static method to be chosen polymorphically when it never will be.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The bank has a base launcher class and a specialized subclass launcher, and a developer assumed the subclass's main would override the parent's and be chosen automatically. This is exactly the misunderstanding that static methods cannot be overridden.

Problem 2 — To show the difference, a static method is called through both a parent-typed and a child-typed reference, revealing that the reference type, not the object, decides which static method runs. This is exactly static method hiding resolved at compile time.

Problem 3 — The same experiment is repeated with a genuine instance method to show real overriding, where the object's actual type decides, highlighting the contrast. This is exactly dynamic dispatch for instance methods.

The code defines a `BaseLauncher` with a static main-like method and an instance method, a `SpecialLauncher` subclass that hides the static one and overrides the instance one, and a `MainOverrideDemo` driver that prints which method runs through different references.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
main-override-demo/
├── src/
│   └── main/java/com/bank/batch/
│       ├── BaseLauncher.java      (static describe() + instance settle())
│       ├── SpecialLauncher.java   (HIDES static describe(), OVERRIDES settle())
│       └── MainOverrideDemo.java  (driver — shows hiding vs overriding)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/batch/BaseLauncher.java \
             src/main/java/com/bank/batch/SpecialLauncher.java \
             src/main/java/com/bank/batch/MainOverrideDemo.java

# Run the demo driver
java -cp out com.bank.batch.MainOverrideDemo

# Run each launcher class directly — the JVM uses THAT class's static main:
java -cp out com.bank.batch.BaseLauncher      # → BaseLauncher.main()
java -cp out com.bank.batch.SpecialLauncher   # → SpecialLauncher.main()
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a SpecialLauncher object assigned to a BaseLauncher reference, used to call both a static method and an instance method.

Step 1 — The driver creates a SpecialLauncher object but stores it in a BaseLauncher-typed reference. This sets up the classic test of whether dispatch follows the reference type or the object type.

Step 2 — For the static describe method, the program shows that a static call is resolved by the declared type, not the object. Calling through the BaseLauncher type runs BaseLauncher's describe, and calling through the SpecialLauncher type runs SpecialLauncher's describe. The two static methods coexist; one hides the other, and selection happens at compile time by type.

Step 3 — For the instance settle method, the program creates a plain BaseLauncher and a SpecialLauncher held in a BaseLauncher reference. Calling settle on the base object runs the base version, as expected.

Step 4 — Calling settle on the special object, even though the reference is typed as BaseLauncher, runs SpecialLauncher's overriding version. This is dynamic dispatch: the runtime looks at the actual object type and chooses the overriding method, which is true overriding and the opposite of static hiding.

Step 5 — The contrast is now explicit: the static method's outcome depended on the reference type and compile-time selection, while the instance method's outcome depended on the object type and runtime selection. Applied to main, which is static, there is no overriding at all, and running a particular launcher class simply invokes that class's own static main.

Step 6 — Running each launcher class directly on the command line confirms the point: the JVM invokes BaseLauncher's main when you name BaseLauncher, and SpecialLauncher's main when you name SpecialLauncher, selected by the class name, never by polymorphism.

```
Oct 30, 2026 5:10:19 PM com.bank.batch.MainOverrideDemo main
INFO: Static call via BaseLauncher.describe()    = BaseLauncher.describe() [static — bound to BaseLauncher]
INFO: Static call via SpecialLauncher.describe() = SpecialLauncher.describe() [static — HIDES BaseLauncher's]
INFO: Instance call base.settle():
INFO: BaseLauncher.settle() [instance — base settlement]
INFO: Instance call special.settle() (overridden despite Base reference):
INFO: SpecialLauncher.settle() [instance — OVERRIDES base, special settlement]
INFO: Conclusion: static main() is HIDDEN by subclasses, never OVERRIDDEN.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  object: new SpecialLauncher()
    │
    ├─ STATIC describe()  → resolved by REFERENCE TYPE (compile time)
    │     BaseLauncher.describe()    → Base's version
    │     SpecialLauncher.describe() → Special's version   (HIDING, not override)
    │
    └─ INSTANCE settle()  → resolved by OBJECT TYPE (runtime, dynamic dispatch)
          BaseLauncher ref → SpecialLauncher object
                │
                ▼ virtual dispatch
          SpecialLauncher.settle()   (true OVERRIDE)

  main() is STATIC → same as describe():
    java BaseLauncher    → BaseLauncher.main()     ← chosen by class NAME
    java SpecialLauncher → SpecialLauncher.main()  ← chosen by class NAME
    NO polymorphism, NO overriding — only hiding
```

  │  + static main(String[]): void │  HIDES

  └───────────────────────────────┘

  1. BaseLauncher.describe()    → Base version (type-bound)
  2. SpecialLauncher.describe() → Special version (type-bound)

sections.s6_takeaway:
No, the main method cannot be overridden, and the reason is that overriding applies only to instance methods while main is static. Overriding is a runtime mechanism: when a subclass provides an instance method with the same signature as its superclass, a call through a superclass reference is dispatched dynamically to the subclass version based on the actual object. That is polymorphism. Static methods are bound to the class rather than to any object, so they are excluded from this mechanism entirely.

What actually happens when a subclass declares a static method with the same signature as the parent's is called hiding, not overriding. The two static methods coexist as separate members, and which one runs is decided at compile time by the type of the reference, not by the runtime type of any object. So if a parent has a static method and a child hides it, calling through the parent type runs the parent's version even when the object is a child, which is exactly the opposite of overriding. Applied to main, a subclass can declare its own static main, but it merely hides the parent's; it does not override it.

Crucially, there is no polymorphism in the JVM entry-point mechanism at all. The launcher does not do dynamic dispatch; it simply invokes the static main of precisely the class you named on the command line. Run the parent class and the parent's main runs; run the child class and the child's main runs. Each is chosen by the class name, which is a static, type-based selection, never a runtime object-based one. In our banking tools each runnable launcher class just has its own main, and this lack of overriding is actually a good thing, because it guarantees that running a specific launcher predictably runs that class's own startup logic.

The senior tells I mention are these. The at-Override annotation is the quickest check: putting it on a static method that only hides a parent's static method is a compile error, because at-Override asserts genuine overriding, which static methods cannot do. Hiding is generally discouraged for ordinary static methods precisely because it looks like overriding but behaves differently, which confuses readers. And you cannot flip a method between static and instance across a hierarchy, so main stays static throughout. The clean mental model I keep is that instance methods override and are chosen by the object at runtime, static methods hide and are chosen by the reference type at compile time, and main, being static, is therefore never overridden, only hidden, with the JVM always calling the named class's own static main.

---

keyPoints: No — static methods cannot be overridden, only hidden
Child class can declare its own static main — method hiding
JVM entry point is determined by the class name, not inheritance
Static method hiding vs instance method overriding is a key distinction
